Russia used the new 9M723-2 ballistic missile, known as the “Iskander-1000,” against Kyiv for the first time during one of the summer missile strikes, according to Ukraine’s Main Directorate of Intelligence (HUR).
Ukraine claims that the missile is part of the “Bora-M” system and has a reported range of up to 550 km, although earlier reports claimed a range of up to 1,000 km. The increased range is reportedly achieved through a larger, more energy-dense solid-fuel motor, which also required modifications to the launcher.
According to open-source claims, the missile may have a range of up to 1,000–1,300 km, with the additional propellant increasing the motor’s volume by around 10–15%. To accommodate the increased fuel capacity, the warhead is reportedly reduced to approximately 300–350 kg, compared with the standard 480 kg warhead of the Iskander-M.
The missile is capable of carrying high-explosive fragmentation or cluster warheads and may feature enhanced maneuverability during the terminal phase, including evasive maneuvers at loads of approximately 20–30 g. It is also equipped or intended to be equipped with onboard electronic warfare systems and countermeasures such as chaff and thermal flares.
The existence of an upgraded Iskander-M missile with a reported range of up to 1,000 km, hence its unofficial designation “Iskander-1000,” was first reported in July 2024. In December 2025, Ukrainian sources unofficially reported that the missile had already been used at a range of up to 800 km.
In October 2025, Ukrainian sources published leaked Russian procurement documents indicating the planned production of 18 ballistic missiles under the designation 9M723-2.
The missile is fitted with a combined guidance system, using inertial guidance during the initial and mid-course phases and an electro-optical/thermal-imaging seeker during the terminal phase. Its reported accuracy is claimed to be as high as 5 meters CEP.

High-resolution satellite imagery of the third Type 054B frigate for the People’s Liberation Army Navy (PLAN).
The image clearly shows a 48-cell vertical launch system (VLS) for surface-to-air missiles, as well as larger midship anti-ship missile launchers compared to the first two Type 054B frigates, which have 32 VLS cells and smaller midship anti-ship missile launchers.

The U.S. Army has tested the M2A4 Bradley IFV as a carrier for FireAnt unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs) mounted along its sides.
The small FireAnt UGV weighs just 27 kg and can carry electronic warfare (EW) and electronic intelligence (ELINT) equipment, or be used as a kamikaze UGV. The long-term goal is for these drones to operate as part of a swarm.
During the Pegasus Charge 3 exercise at Fort Hood, Texas, the FireAnt was demonstrated as a kamikaze UGV, intended to finish off vehicles disabled by small-arms fire. In theory, it could also be used against enemy fortifications or troops sheltering in bunkers while the Bradley provides suppressive fire.
However, this concept raises some concerns in the context of the war in Ukraine. The FireAnts occupy the space normally used for the Bradley's side-mounted reactive armor, reducing the vehicle's protection. They also appear to require manual deployment by the crew or dismounted troops, which could be impractical during an active assault.
Still, the idea of using existing combat vehicles to quickly deliver UGVs to the front line is interesting. It just needs further development and refinement.
The Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) carried out drone strikes on a fuel depot belonging to the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in the border town of Adikong, West Darfur, near the Chad border.
A ballistic missile launched by Ansar Allah (Houthis) struck a position belonging to Saudi-backed forces in Al Khawkhah District, Al-Hudaydah Governorate, western Yemen.

Italy has approved a military aid package worth around €3 billion for Ukraine. The package includes four SAMP/T NG air-defense systems, Aster 30 interceptor missiles, and seven long-range radars produced by France’s Thales and Italy’s Leonardo, aimed at strengthening Ukraine’s defenses against ballistic missiles.
Some of the missiles are expected to be delivered by October, with the package funded through the EU’s Ukraine Support Loan program.

Ukraine carried out a large-scale, combined missile strike on Donetsk today, using a mix of FP-5 Flamingo cruise missiles, Storm Shadow/SCALP-EG cruise missiles, and potentially another unidentified munition. Two separate targets were struck.
Six missiles hit an underground parking facility at an unfinished residential complex, while another seven struck an industrial building. Ukrainian channels claim both locations were being used to store large quantities of military equipment, including missile and rocket launchers, armored vehicles, and personnel.
Several fragments with folded wings, typically associated with glide bombs and jet-powered stand-off munitions, were recovered. Based on the surviving markings, at least some of the munitions used in the strike have been identified as Storm Shadow/SCALP-EG cruise missiles.
One fragment bears a manufacturer’s plate marked MBDA FRANCE, along with the manufacturer code F0555. Another fragment contains a toothed mechanism, serial number 10625, and the date 20.08.2024. This is likely part of the mechanism used to deploy or control the missile’s wing.
As for the unidentified munition, one possibility is a weapon developed under the U.S. Extended-Range Attack Missile (ERAM) program. However, no confirmed photographs of an intact ERAM missile have emerged so far, making this identification highly speculative.
Another possibility is the AGM-158A JASSM air-launched cruise missile.
